hidden_items.why: Taking the address of the local `slot` may cause the implementation to move its storage from the stack to the heap. A Go call can panic, and a panic unwinds the calling goroutine out of the enclosing function, running deferred functions on the way (Go spec 'Handling panics'). Nothing at `f(x)` marks that possibility: Go has no `try`, no `throws` clause, no propagation operator and no checked-failure annotation of any kind, and the callee's declaration is outside the local site. The failure is reachable within the probe's declared input domain because the domain places no constraint on `f`'s body. Recorded once as a distinct event at local site 2.

(1) `put := func(p *int32) { *p = 12 }` is a one-parameter function that takes writable access to a caller-owned signed 32-bit integer variable and whose body is exactly that one assignment. Go's pointer parameter IS the form the language conventionally uses for this purpose: Go 1.26 Language Specification 'Address operators' fixes that `*p` denotes the variable pointed to, and a variable is assignable, so a *int32 parameter is writable access with no opt-out. (3) `put(&cell)` uses Go's required explicit address-of form at the call site together with the pointer parameter and the written dereference in the body - all three of the places the task allows the explicit form to live. (4) `return cell` reads `cell` after the call; the observable result is 12. Wrapping the integer in a mutable container or a struct was NOT used, so the P-a exclusion the task names does not apply. determinacy_enumeration: Interpretation 1 - `xs` is a non-empty sequence of int32: A1 = values copied throughout while the closure shares `k`, A2 = no caller-observable mutation (the fragment writes only `ys` and `v`, both declared inside it), A4 = fixed-width signed integer, A8 = allocation occurs at the first `append`, A9 = the loop runs to completion and the fragment returns normally. WITNESS: the frozen probe itself, built and run under `go build -o BIN FILE.go`, printing -1.

Interpretation 2 - `xs` is empty: every element above is unchanged except A9, where the loop body never runs, `ys` is still the nil slice at `ys[0]`, and the fragment exits by PANICKING and unwinding rather than returning. WITNESS: the identical fragment with `xs := []int32{}` in the surrounding program panics with 'runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0'. This is the only materially different reading the fragment admits, and it exists because `xs` is given context outside the measured fragment. EXCLUDED CLASSES with citation and the refutation Rule 1.3.1.e requires: (a) A8 = 'no allocation occurs' - EXCLUDED, `var ys []int32` is the nil slice (spec 'The zero value', 'Slice types') so the first append must allocate; refutation witness: a program printing cap(ys) before and after the first append shows 0 then 8. (b) A1 = 'the closure copies k' - EXCLUDED by Go spec 'Function literals' ('shared between the surrounding function and the function literal'); refutation witness: a variant that sets k = 10 after the literal is created makes neg(1) return 9 instead of -1, which a copy could not produce. (c) A2 = 'the fragment may mutate xs' - excluded: the range clause copies each element into `v` (spec 'For statements with range clause') and nothing in the fragment assigns to an element of `xs`; refutation witness: a variant that prints xs after the loop shows 1 2 3 unchanged. (d) A9 = 'may suspend/resume later' - NOT REALIZABLE, flagged LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE: Go has no async/await, no coroutine and no suspension point in an ordinary call; concurrency is entered only by a written `go` statement or a channel operation, neither of which appears. (e) A7 = 'the operator is user-redefinable' - NOT REALIZABLE, LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE: Go has no operator overloading, so `k - a` cannot run user code. (f) A1 = non-call/token substitution - NOT REALIZABLE, LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE (no macro facility). (g) A10 = 'undefined / trapping / build-mode-dependent overflow' - excluded, spec 'Integer overflow' fixes wraparound with no build mode that changes it.

locality_detail.hop: variable decl (VAR): the declaration of `xs`, which the probe places in given context outside the measured fragment
locality_detail.required_for_fact: control_flow_effect and type_and_representation - the number of iterations, and therefore whether `ys[0]` returns a value or panics, is decided by `xs`'s length; and although the fragment pins the ELEMENT type indirectly (the range value flows into a func(int32) parameter, and Go requires identical types), the operand's own type - slice versus array, and its length - is in its declaration. One declaration resolves both, so H_i is 1 by the minimality rule 2.3.2. `k`'s declaration is NOT a required hop: Go spec 'Arithmetic operators' requires both operands of `k - a` to be of identical type and `a` is written as int32, so k's type is pinned by the fragment itself. `append`'s behaviour is NOT a hop either: it is a builtin whose contract is stated in the language specification ('Appending to and copying slices'), which Rule 2.2.3 makes zero-cost knowledge. No G-hop arises: the fragment names no implementation-sized type and Go exposes no arithmetic-safety build mode.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H2 - Hidden writable aliasing or mutation
hidden_items.why: At local site 1 the function literal captures `k` by REFERENCE: Go spec 'Function literals' says the referenced variables 'are then shared between the surrounding function and the function literal', so the closure holds a live handle to `k`'s storage. Go has no capture list, no `[&k]`/`[k]` distinction, no `move` keyword and no copy-capture form, so nothing at the local site says whether the closure holds a value or a shared variable - and the two are materially different on the observable-result dimension. Verified: a variant that assigns k = 10 after the literal is created makes neg(1) return 9 rather than -1. The assignment-target exclusion does not apply (`k` is not being assigned here) and the local-token exclusion does not apply (there is no token).

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: At local site 1 the function literal may allocate: a closure that escapes is heap-allocated, and the captured variable `k` is moved from the enclosing function's frame to the heap so that it can be shared. Both decisions are made by an escape analysis over the whole program and neither is named at the site - there is no `new`, no composite literal, no `make` and no allocator token. LED fails because the Go reference deliberately does not say where a variable or a closure lives. Charged here and not in Semantic Determinacy exactly as methodology 03 Rule 1.2.2.b directs.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: A second, distinct H4 event at local site 3: `append` allocates a new underlying array and COPIES the existing elements into it when the destination's capacity is insufficient, and silently reslices in place when it is not - 'If it has sufficient capacity, the destination is resliced to accommodate the new elements. If it does not, a new underlying array will be allocated' (Go spec 'Appending to and copying slices'). Which of the two happens is decided by a capacity that is not written at the site, so the LED gate fails: the local site plus the reference do not fix ONE outcome. The consequence is material beyond cost - when append reslices in place, any other slice over the same array sees the write, and when it reallocates, it does not. Verified on the toolchain: capacity goes 0 -> 8 at the first append and the element's address is unchanged at the second. A distinct event from the closure one under section 1.3.2 (different rule, different local site).

complexity_detail.description: Function literal `func(params) results { body }` yields a function value inside a function body.

A function literal is a closure: the variables it refers to from a surrounding function are SHARED with that function, not copied, and they survive as long as they are accessible. Go has no capture list and no copy-capture form.
Short variable declaration `:=` infers the declared type from the right-hand expression.
`var` declaration of a slice type; the zero value of a slice is nil, with length 0, capacity 0 and no underlying array.
complexity_detail.citation: Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'Variable declarations', 'The zero value' and 'Slice types'

complexity_detail.description: `for ... range` means different things for different range expressions; over a slice it evaluates the expression once, yields index and a COPY of each element in increasing index order, produces 0 iterations for a nil slice, and (since Go 1.22) declares the iteration variables anew in each iteration.
complexity_detail.citation: Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'For statements with range clause'

complexity_detail.description: The blank identifier `_` may be assigned to but introduces no binding, and is how an unwanted range value is discarded.

`append` returns a new slice and either reslices the destination in place, when capacity suffices, or allocates a new underlying array and copies, when it does not - so the result must be assigned back and may or may not share storage with the argument.
complexity_detail.citation: Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'Appending to and copying slices'

complexity_detail.description: Call expression on a function value, used at an argument position.
Binary `-` requires both operand types to be identical; Go performs no implicit numeric promotion, so the operand types must be made to agree explicitly.
Integer overflow wraps: the result exists, is deterministically defined by the two's-complement representation, and does not cause a run-time panic, in every build mode.
Index-bounds checking on a slice happens at run time and an out-of-range index causes a run-time panic, whereas a constant index into an array is checked at compile time.
complexity_detail.citation: Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'Index expressions' and 'Run-time panics'

complexity_detail.description: `return expr` terminates the enclosing function and supplies its result; a function with no result parameters may return by falling off its end.
